en: The Reality of Gaṇapati //0// May there be no obstacle! Oṃ, homage to the Perfected One! Oṃ!

Gaṇapati, the teacher of the hosts of gods, the bestower of success upon Gaṅgā and Umā, and the son [of Śiva], asked Śiva for the sake of the glory of the light of the power and virility [of his father]. (1) 1. "O Lord Śiva, please tell me, O Lord Gaṇa: I am the son of Your Honor; I ask Your Honor, my father—grant me this boon, my father: that I may know how to discern the nature of the five deities, and from where their discernment originates; grant me this boon, my father."

2. The Lord said: "I am Gaṇapati, free from attachment, beyond the reach of speech and mind. This sound is empty; it arises from the *oṃkāra* as a *bindu*, like the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, appearing like the sun, or like incense smoke. It blazes with the form of a mass of stars. From that *bindu* were born the five deities: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Kama, and the venerable Sadāśiva. Thus am I, the one who brings about the manifestation of the divine self."
3. Gaṇapati said: "O son of the Lord of the World! Come forth once more into the light of the world; let the noble Rahadyan, the son of the Lord of the World, know you."
4. The Lord said:

I am Gaṇapati; I am the supreme Lord who dwells within the essence of the world. From the five-fold divine self (*pañcadaivātmā*), the five subtle elements (*pañcatanmātra*) arise. Their forms are as follows: from Brahmā arises smell (*gandha*); from Viṣṇu arises taste (*rasa*); from Rudra arises form (*rūpa*); from Me arises touch (*sparśa*); and from the venerable Sadāśiva arises sound (*śabda*). Furthermore, from sound arises space (*ākāśa*). Its form is such that its color is like pure crystal. From touch arises wind (*vāyu*); its form is *vī*, white and colorless. From form arises fire (*teja*); its form is *nī*, white in color. Then, from taste arises water (*āpah*); its form is *o*, with a dark (*kṛṣṇa*) color. From smell arises earth (*pṛthivī*); its form is *oṃ*, with a yellow (*pīta*) color. Its seed-syllable (*akṣara*) is *nakāra*; it is the *oṃkāra* of the scripture of life. Furthermore, O Gaṇapati, from earth arises the ground (*bhūmi*); from water arises the ocean (*vvai*); from fire arise the sun, the moon, and the stars; from wind arises the breeze; from space arises sound; and from the world arise the stationary beings (*sthāvara*)—grass, trees, creepers, shrubs, and bamboos—as well as the moving beings (*jaṅgama*)—livestock, birds, fish, and cows. Such is the variety of the world.

Gaṇapati said: "O son of the Lord of the World! For you have already been instructed by the Lord regarding all knowledge concerning the reality of the worlds; now, furthermore, O child of the Lord, you must become one who possesses great wisdom in discerning the nature of human beings."
6. The Lord said:

O King of the Assembly, that which is the origin of humans is the same as the origin of gods and the origin of the world, because human beings arise from the *bindu*, the primary root of the *oṃkāra*. What is its form? Brahmā made his body of action (*kārya-śarīra*); that which was made was earth and water. Viṣṇu made his body of perception; that which was made was fire. We (the Rudras) made our body of breath; that which was made was touch. The venerable Sadāśiva made his body of sound; that which was made was space. Such am I; such is the form of the self at birth.
7. Gaṇapati said:

“O Lord, together with the supreme lord of the planets, there is the section concerning the world and human beings. Previously, O noble Lord, you spoke of the station of the divine self within the body and its existence within the world.”

8. Īśvara said: O Gaṇādhipa, who is Anaku? Maṅke Piṛṅvākna Pavarah is one with you. Regarding the state of the *daivātmā* (divine self) within the body: for birth and the world are one; that which is birth is the world. What is its form? In the southern part of the world, Brahmā resides; he protects the earth. Viṣṇu resides in the northern part; he protects the waters. Rudra resides in the western part; he protects the sun, the moon, and the stars. We reside in the eastern part; we protect the wind. The venerable Sadāśiva resides in the center; he protects space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, regarding birth: Brahmā is situated in the *mūlādhāra*; he protects passion (*rāga*), maintains it in the nostrils, and causes the perception of smell. Viṣṇu is situated in the navel; he protects the body, maintains it in the tongue, and causes the perception of taste. Rudra is situated in the heart; he protects the waking state (*jāgra*), maintains it in the palate, and causes the perception of consciousness. We are situated in the throat; we protect speech (*āturu*), maintain it in the lips, and cause the perception of sound. The venerable Sadāśiva is situated at the tip of the tongue; he protects all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñāna*), maintains it in the ears, and causes the perception of voice. Such is the form of the *daivātmā* within the body, and likewise in the higher worlds.
Gaṇapati said:

O son of the Lord, now there exists a boar that is the body of the Lord; it resides in the union of the *mūlādhāra*, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the tip of the tongue—the sprout of the Son of the Lord.
10. The Lord said:

I am Gaṇapati. Listen well to this secret teaching of our Lord concerning the reality of that which is meditated upon at the *mūlādhāra*. It is situated between the anus and the genitals. Its color is like the dawn (*aruṇa*); it is four-cornered and its base is downward-facing. Within it is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) SKAḤ, with eight *lava*s. Inside the SKAḤ is a jewel (*maṇi*) with a color like lightning. Inside the lightning-like jewel is the syllable OṂ. The vital air (*vāyu*) rises from there toward the *śivadvāra* (the aperture of Śiva). From the *śivadvāra* it rises to the nose; from the nose it rises to the tip of the tongue. It blocks the seven gates. Its opening is at the throat. From the throat it enters the heart, blocking the entire body. Such is the form of the *mūlādhāra*. Above the *mūlādhāra* is the place called the navel (*nābhi*). Its depth is sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅguli*). Its color is like the SKAḤ with ten *lava*s. Inside the SKAḤ is something like the rising sun. Inside that which is like the rising sun is *amṛta* (nectar), which supports the intestines and the stomach. Above the navel, its depth is eight finger-breadths. This is the heart. Its color is like a straight-pointed star with thirty-one *lava*s. It is surrounded by fire. Inside the fire is the sun; inside the sun is the moon; inside the moon is the white (*śukla*) color, like a lotus seed. Inside the white is the *prāṇavāyu*; inside the *prāṇa* is the *prāṇaliṅga*. Above the heart, its depth is sixteen finger-breadths. This is the throat (*kaṇṭha*). Its color is like a straight-pointed white star with ten *lava*s. Inside the straight-pointed white star is something like a lotus seed. Furthermore, above the throat, its depth is sixteen finger-breadths. This is the tip of the tongue. It is like a curved hook (*kucup*), multicolored. Inside the curved hook is the *bindusāramaṇi* (jewel of the essence of the point). Inside the *bindusāramaṇi* is pure crystal (*śuddhasphaṭika*). Inside the pure crystal is the Void (*śūnya*), which is Nirvāṇa. Such is the form of the five colors.

11. Gaṇapati said: "O son of the Lord, you are most excellent among us; therefore, O excellent Lord, grant me this boon: that I may cause all those born together with me to be reborn at the time of our union. Grant this boon, O noble brother."
12. The Lord said:

And as for me, O Gaṇapati, my limbs are manifest; thus there is the birth that causes the manifestation of all births. It is just like this, brother: the body is merely the instrument for the act of procreation. Through the union of the subtle form, the *ātman* appears; it is white (*śukla*), its color like a pure crystal gem. It manifests from the primary limb (*pradhāna-aṅga*) and is manifested by the syllable *oṃ*. Both forms are equal when they emerge together into the mother’s womb, yet their nature is distinct: one is of the form of the aggregate (*piṇḍākṛti*), because it shares the same color as the semen and blood, while the other is produced by the *oṃkāra*, possessing a subtle form, which is brought forth by the activity of the *oṃkāra*.

13. As for the form of the sequence of the *patmahanya* (the sixfold lotus): the first [digit] is the *matmahan vṛh* (the great womb); the *matmahan vṛh* is like a *mpĕhan* (a small jar), its color is white (*varṇṇanya*). The third digit is that *mpĕhan*, its form is a single-pointed *hantiga*. Its color is red (*rakta*), it is the *matmahan rah*. The fifth digit is the *aṇḍa* (egg), which is the *matmahan śivaliṅga*; it is globular in the middle, pierced by the syllable *oṃkāra*, and possesses a subtle form (*sūkṣmarūpa*). The sixth digit is the *śivaliṅga*, which is the *matmahan māyārekhā*. The seventh digit is the *māyārekhā*, which is the *matmahan agni* (fire). The eighth digit is that *agni*, which is the *matmahan* like a young child (*anak gaḍiṅ*). From the ninth digit, that young child, there arises the breath (*uśvāsa*) from the *oṃkāra*: nails, teeth, hair, body-hair, and the sense-faculties (*gnĕpva*)—these ten digits constitute the yoga. Then the limbs (*tandva*) arise from the womb of its mother. Such is its form, like that of Gaṇapati.
14. Gaṇapati said: "O son of the Lord, please grant me a boon now, O Lord. Grant me this boon, O Prince: that I may enter the womb of a woman and subsequently emerge from it."
15. The Lord said:

Oṃ! Anaku, O Lord of the Assembly! Whatever has been attained by you, do not harbor any doubt. Listen to me regarding that which is hidden within the essence of the Śivaliṅga. "Śiva" is the name for Oṃkāra; "Liṅga" is the name for the white and the dark (the union of Śukla and Śveta). Together they form the complete Śivaliṅga. It is neither great nor small; its form is subtle. When it reaches ten units, it abides in emptiness (*śūnya*). Furthermore, at the time of its flickering, it abides in Nirvāṇa. When one knows this, the mental states (*bape*) disappear, and Nirvāṇa arises. When one abides in Jīva, once the state of Jīva has disappeared, Ātmā arises. That indeed is what is called "living" (*kaorip*).
16. Gaṇapati said:
"O son of the Lord, there is a boon from the Lord for one whose life is about to vanish; it shall come to an end—this is the boon of the Lord."
17. The Lord said:

"O Gaṇapati, I am weary; this burden upon me is exceedingly great and endless. O Noble One, you are my refuge; you are my support and my fulfillment. May you bestow virtue upon me. Now, may you find joy in tasting [this]. We shall conceal ourselves: the disappearance of the *ātman*, the departure into the *jīva*; the disappearance of the *jīva*, the departure into *nirvāṇa*; the disappearance of *nirvāṇa*, the departure into the *śūnya*; the disappearance of the *śūnya*, the departure into the *sūkṣmarūpa*; the disappearance of the *sūkṣmarūpa*, the departure into the state of the Holy One who possesses the *mṅā* (the power of transformation). His station is at the summit of space. The disappearance of the Holy One who possesses the *mṅā*, the departure into the essence of the *niṣkala*."
18. Gaṇapati said:
"O son of the Lord, how is it that the Lord has been hidden? Alas, this name 'the foremost of the sky'—that is the place of the venerable Namuci! Alas, the Lord has abandoned me."
19. The Lord said:

Lift me up, O Gaṇapati! That which is called the "foremost" (agra) in the space of the *liṅganāda* is the single path (*babahan*) that leads upward; its name is the path of the *puruṣa*. This is the way of the venerable Śivātman. Furthermore, when one reaches the end at the navel, his form is like steaming rice. The venerable Śivātman proceeds straight from the navel toward the *śivamaṇḍala*. The *śivamaṇḍala* is defined as bliss (*sukha*) free from suffering, auspiciousness free from evil, where there is no inherent nature (*svabhāva*) such as this—that is the *śivamaṇḍala*. Furthermore, there are the five aspects of the Self (*pañcātmā*), namely: Ātmā, Parātmā, Antarātmā, Nirātmā, and Śūnyātmā. These are all unified with the Śivātman. The venerable Śivātman oversees the path that has been entered, proceeding straight toward the inner space. His color is like scattered gold dust; that is the excellent, firm path. This is the destination of the path. It is auspicious, hidden, and when reached, it is the end. Do not be negligent, my child; this is the secret of the inner self.
Gaṇapati said:
"O son of my lord, this is truly so; now indeed, O boar, descend! Enter the womb of the earth to become the Lord."
21. The Lord said:

Oṃ! Anaku saṅ gaṇapati, maṅke kami avarahe anaku. That which is called the *irikaṅ* is the venerable Tryātmā; it is the meaning of the words of the verse (*śloka*). Inhalation, exhalation, and their union—these are known as the threefold self (*ātmatrayam*).
The three Śivas, the state of the three Puruṣas, and emptiness are indeed one with the single self. (2)
I have no other refuge but Gaṇapati.

Now follows the sequence of the Holy Threefold Self (*tryātmā*). Its forms are: inhalation (*śvāsa*), exhalation (*niḥśvāsa*), and conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Inhalation is the wind that moves upward; exhalation is the wind that moves downward; conjunction is when both winds meet. These three taken together are called the "Threefold Self" (*tryātmā*); it is also known as the "Triple Śiva" (*triśiva*) and the "Triple Puruṣa" (*tripuruṣa*). Furthermore, the "Single Self" (*ekātmā*) is the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*). Moreover, these three selves are non-dual; that indeed is what is called the "Self" (*ātman*). Now, O Gaṇapati, there is that which is called the "Holy Instruction" (*upadeśa*). Its forms are as follows: * *Śvāsa* (Inhalation): The state of drawing the breath upward. * *Niḥśvāsa* (Exhalation): The state of releasing the breath downward. * *Saṃyoga* (Conjunction): The union of the two breaths. These three combined constitute the "Threefold Self. It is also termed the "Triple Śiva" and the "Triple Puruṣa. Furthermore, the "Single Self" is the Great Void. Indeed, these three selves are one and the same; that is precisely what is designated as the "Self. Furthermore, O Gaṇapati, there exists that which is called the "Holy Instruction," the nature of which is as follows: (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly after introducing the concept of the "Instruction" (*upadeśa*). The subsequent section would typically detail the specific meditative or ritual procedures associated with this instruction.)
Withdrawal of the senses, meditation, breath control, concentration, reflection, and absorption—this is said to be the sixfold yoga. (3)
This is what is called the Six-Limbed Yoga (Ṣaḍaṅgayoga). O Gaṇapati, I shall explain it to you. Its forms are: Pratyāhārayoga, Dhyānayoga, Prāṇāyāmayoga, Dhāraṇayoga, Tarkayoga, and Samādhiyoga.
Having diligently withdrawn the senses from their objects—the sense-fields—with a tranquil mind, this is declared to be *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). (4)

The yoga of withdrawal (*pratyāhārayoga*) means: restraining all the sense faculties so that they do not yield to their respective objects; the mind becomes firmly established and tranquil when there is pleasure in its own state, having turned away from its objects. That is the yoga of withdrawal.
That form which is meditated upon constantly—free from dualities, free from change, unattached, and likewise immovable—is called *dhyāna*. (5)

The meaning of *dhyānayoga* is: that which is still, neither changing nor transforming; it is pleasant within the heart; it is unwavering; it is radiant and free from obstruction; its characteristic is the recollection of a single-pointed mind (*ekacittānusmaraṇa*). That indeed is *dhyānayoga*.
Having closed all the gates [of the senses], one directs the breath outward;
having pierced the head with the breath, this is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*. (6)

The yoga of breath control (prāṇāyāmayoga) means closing all the gates: the eyes, the nostrils, the ears, and the mouth. Then, the breath that has arisen should be held within the crown of the head. However, when the practitioner speaks, he should release it through both nostrils, yet the breath must remain balanced; this is indeed prāṇāyāmayoga.
Having established the syllable Oṃ in the heart as being of the nature of Śiva when dissolved into reality, one who is of the nature of emptiness hears nothing; this is called dhāraṇā. (7)

The meaning of *dhāraṇā-yoga* is as follows: the syllable *oṃ*, the *praṇava*, resides in the heart; that is indeed *dhāraṇā*, the mindfulness of the breath. When it disappears into the *kaṛö* (the cranial aperture) at the time of *yoga*, that is the Lord whose nature is the void (*śūnya-śiva-ātmaka*); that is *dhāraṇā-yoga*.
The mind is pure like space, yet in reality it is not space itself; for the ultimate truth is beyond words, and thus the application of reasoning is prescribed. (8)

The meaning of *tarkayoga* (the yoga of reasoning) is as follows: it is like the sky, which is the Lord Paramārtha; there is no path [to it], because there is no sound therein. That alone is the sign of Paramārtha, which is utterly beyond all doubt; it is the ultimate goal in the midst of the waters. That indeed is *tarkayoga*.
That which is without equanimity, without characteristics, without support, without longing, without obscuration, and without anything to be accomplished—that is declared to be *samādhi*. (9)

The meaning of *samādhiyoga* is this: it is knowledge that does not neglect, does not conceptualize, does not grasp, has no desire therein, has no goal to be achieved, and is radiant and free from obscuration; that indeed is *samādhiyoga*.
Kāmbalantā and hṛnmūla; tiktā and kṛṣṇā would certainly be dhruva.
Atikṛṣṇānta is the abode of Śiva, the Lord of the World. (10)
Within the center of the heart, there is indeed a vein; its length is very long. I am that Lord Lokanātha; my master is Lord Śiva.

Whether one adopts one's own characteristic mark or the characteristic mark of another, that twice-born man who acts thus dissolves himself among all beings; his own characteristic mark is dissolved. (11)

Thus spoke the twice-born: "He merges his own *liṅga* with that supreme *liṅga*. He dissolves into the very source from which he was born; there is no difference in the heart of the forest [of existence], for there exists only the one *svaliṅga*. He is dissolved within all beings, beginning with Brahmā; therefore, he is made to merge into his own *liṅga*."
That which has arisen spontaneously for oneself and is worshipped by oneself alone, having first arisen as its own characteristic, is called the *ātmaliṅga* by the wise. (12)
Thus it is said to awaken the consciousness of the self: "The head is the heart; the head is the place of worship; for that head is the *ātma-liṅga*, which is the *liṅga* of the wise one."
Thousands of Śiva-liṅgas are not equal to the self-liṅga;
there are none superior to it, for the self-liṅga is preeminent. (13)
Regarding the Kaliṅga [lingas]: how many are the noble Lord Ātmaliṅgas? They are indeed singular and unique; he possesses one thousand lingas, for he is the Viśeṣaliṅga.
Thousands of golden liṅgas are not equal to one’s own liṅga;
thousands of eye-liṅgas are not equal to the Śiva-liṅga. (14)
The number of *liṅgas* made of metal is ninety; they do not equal the solitary *ātmaliṅga*. Although the number of *akṣiliṅgas* is ninety, they are not equal to the *śivaliṅga*.
That which is joined with the three-syllable words is declared to be the syllable *oṃ*;
it arises from the *liṅga*, is established in the mind, and is the most excellent Śiva-liṅga. (15)

Furthermore, it is said that the Holy One resides within the *ātmaliṅga*, namely this *oṃkāra* and the *tryakṣara*. He is indeed perceived within the *liṅga* as the mind’s goal; he is the supreme *śivaliṅga*.
For the twice-born, the deity is in the waters; for the sages, it is in heaven;
for the worlds, it is a fragment of stone; but for the silent ones, the Self alone is the deity. (16)

Furthermore, O twice-born one, regarding the Vai: the deity resides within them. Regarding the Ṛṣis in heaven: the deity resides within them. Regarding the world, in the case of the *arccaliṅga*, the image, and the stone: the deity resides within them. Furthermore, as for that which grows—the noble *ātman* is its deity.
Those who, deluded regarding their own signs, should adopt the signs of others, and those who, out of delusion, worship [them], shall obtain no fruit whatsoever. (17)
The practitioner who has abandoned the external linga and performs worship with his own body attains the fruit of the *kḍik*.
Kamala, Praṇāla, Tiktaka, and Liṅga—Maheśvara should be installed there in that divine temple of the body. (18)

That which is the subtle succession (paruparu) is called Kamala; it is the supreme abode, the ultimate limit of that which is sought after as divine. Therein resides Lord Śiva as the foundation (pratiṣṭhā).
This Maheśvara, the size of a thumb and crystal-like in appearance, is to be meditated upon there within the divine abode of the body. (19)

Where is that bitter [taste]? Its measure is the size of the thumb; its power is like that of Lord Īśvara, as clear as crystal. This body is equal to the paryyaṅkan posture; here indeed one should always worship the Lord.
If your mind is engaged in reflection, this is declared to be the bitter [result];
yet one becomes a powerful king whose domain is as vast as the seven continents. (20)

As for that which possesses arms and speaks its own nature, it is the one who possesses the tongue; there is the tongue, and there are two tongues. Its thumb is above; there are six together with the seven islands (*nūsa*), because those are the seven continents (*saptadvīpa*). Such is Lord Bhaṭāreśvara; he possesses great power yet is not all-pervasive. This is the meaning of "possessing arms," for it is called so by the wise (*saṅ paṇḍita*).
Viṣṇu is stationed on the left arm, or the four-faced one on the right;
Maheśvara, however, is situated in the middle, while Viṣṇu is within the mind. (21)
Regarding the locations of the venerable Viṣṇu and the venerable Brahmā, they are in Keriṅ; Lord Śiva is situated in the center. In brief: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—these are the Lords.
Thus is the *Saṅ hyaṅ liṅgodbhāva*:
Aṃ Vaṃ Oṃ Naṃ [Yaṃ] Aṃ Maṃ Ñaṃ.
Śiṃ ūṃ maṃ aṃ taṃ
And Śiva eternally resides as the subtle element within the heart;
because he possesses sovereignty within the subtle mind, he is known and remembered as Śiva. (22)
Thus, when the heart is subtle and the mind is subtle, Lord Śiva takes possession; He is recognized through wisdom, and His word, O Lord Śiva, is fulfilled.
Sadāśiva, who resides in the heart, is contemplated at the end of the heart within the secret abode as the void beyond the void; this is called supreme liberation. (23)

The Lord spoke again concerning the cavity of the heart: "In the hollow of the heart, that which is called the *guhyālaya* (the secret abode), which is extremely subtle, the emptiness of emptiness, more minute than the minute—that is the supreme absolute state (*paramakevalya*) and the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). It is a state beyond the reach of pleasure and pain."
With fourteen syllables as blossoms, radiant and fragrant, I constantly worship Śiva, who is established in the station of the heart. (24)

The place within the heart is the abode of Lord Śiva; having finished his worship, he constantly takes refuge in the Holy One of fourteen syllables. Its form is as follows: *saṃ*, *baṃ*, *taṃ*, *aṃ*, *iṃ*, *naṃ*, *maṃ*, *śiṃ*, *vaṃ*, *yaṃ*, *aṃ*, *uṃ*, *maṃ*, *oṃ*. That Holy One of fourteen syllables resides in the *puṣpa sumĕkar* (the flower-spike); one should worship Him continuously with fragrant incense at all times.
From the partless arises sound; from sound, the manifestation of the drop (bindu);
from the drop, the arising of the moon; and from the moon, the universe arises again and again. (25)

The Kaliṅga dissolves into the Niṣkala; from the Niṣkala it dissolves into the Nāda; from the Nāda it dissolves into the Bindu; from the Bindu it dissolves into the Ardhacandra; from the Ardhacandra it dissolves into Viṣṇu, whose characteristic is shimmering and radiant. Viṣṇu is Lord Bhaṭāra Saṅ Hyang Praṇava; the nature of Saṅ Hyang Praṇava is Oṃkāra.
The entire universe, together with the moon and joined with the bindu, is withdrawn into the nāda as one; this is always proclaimed as the syllable Oṃ. (26)

The *viśva* is not joined with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), nor with the point (*bindu*) and the sound (*nāda*). The *praṇava*, the half-moon, the point, and the sound are also combined; this is the great *oṃkāra*.
Everything dissolves into the moon; the moon dissolves into the bindu;
and the bindu dissolves into the nāda—this is the characteristic of the sequence. (27)

The *viśva* emerges from the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); the half-moon dissolves into the point (*bindu*); that point, in turn, emerges into the sound (*nāda*). Such is the characteristic of the principles (*tattva*). Furthermore, that *nāda* returns to the partless (*niṣkala*); the partless is called the principle of illusion (*māyātattva*), for the primary matter (*pradhāna*) is what merges with the *nāda*. Again, that partless returns to the inner void (*śūnyāntara*); that inner void returns to the absolute void (*atyantaśūnya*), which merges with the partless. Furthermore, O Gaṇapati, that which is named as origination, maintenance, and dissolution is the venerable *praṇava*.
The Self is produced from Śiva, and from that Self comes primordial nature (prakṛti); from primordial nature the Sun is born, and from the Sun fire is produced. (28)

The syllable *iṃ* is what is called Śiva; from Śiva arises the *ātman*, *baṃ*; from the *ātman* arises *prakṛti*, *saṃ*; from *prakṛti* arises Āditya, *taṃ*; from Āditya arises Agni, *aṃ*. Such is the origin of the five noble Brahmas (*pañcabrahma*). Their sequence is: *iṃ*, *baṃ*, *saṃ*, *taṃ*, *aṃ*.
The Self rests upon primordial nature, and the Sun likewise rests upon the Self; Fire rests upon the Sun, and Śiva rests upon Fire—thus is stability described. (29)
The origin of these [syllables] is their essential nature: *saṃ*, *baṃ*, *taṃ*, *aṃ*, *iṃ*. This is the state of the five Brahmas; *saṃ*, *baṃ*, *taṃ*, *aṃ*, *iṃ* is their sequence.
Fire dissolves into the sun, and the sun dissolves into primordial nature;
primordial nature dissolves into the Self, and the Self dissolves into Śiva. (30)
Aṃ, tumūt taṃ, tumūt saṃ, tumūt baṃ, tumūt iṃ. Thus is the dissolution of the five Brahmas: aṃ, taṃ, saṃ, baṃ, iṃ; such is their sequence.
The conjunction of the two, the Moon and the Self, is declared to be the letter *a*; the conjunction of the Sun and Fire is considered by the wise to be the letter *u*. (31)
The letter *sa* together with the letter *baṃ* produced the syllable *akāra*. The letter *naṃ* together with the letter *aṃ* produced the syllable *ukāra*.
*Iśāna* became the letter *makāra*, which is in the middle and also above; and the letter *ukāra* is below. They know that the conjunction of these is the syllable *oṃ*. (32)

Īśāna is *iṃ*; that which produces the letter *ma*. Such is the fivefold Brahman (*pañcabrahma*), which produces the three syllables (*tryakṣara*). The conjunction of these three syllables is as follows: that which produces the letter *u* is its manifestation; the letter *a* is placed in the middle, the letter *ma* is above, and the letter *u* is below. Such is the union of the three syllables, which produces the *oṃkāra*.
That which is birth is *ya-va-śi-ma-na*, and that which is abiding is *śi-va-ma-na-ya*;
that which is dissolution is *na-ma-śi-va-ya*. This is remembered as the five-syllable mantra. (33)

Yaṃ, vaṃ, śiṃ, maṃ, naṃ: these are the five-syllable mantra of origination (utpatti). Śiṃ, vaṃ, maṃ, naṃ, yaṃ: these are the five-syllable mantra of persistence (sthiti). Naṃ, maṃ, śiṃ, vaṃ, yaṃ: these are the five-syllable mantra of dissolution (pralīna).
In the first [syllable], there is the elision of *namaḥ* and the letter *a* arises; in the second, there is the elision of *śiva* and the letter *u* indeed arises. (34)
The letter *i* is that which causes disappearance; it enters into the letter *a*. Furthermore, its companion, the letter *u*, causes Śiva to enter into the letter *u*.
In the third [syllable], the letter *ya* is elided and the letter *ma* likewise arises;
through the elision of the letters *a* and *u*, the letter *o* is pronounced. (35)

The letter *ya* of its seed-syllable disappears; the letter *ma* is produced. However, the letter *a* and that letter *u*—that which disappeared when [the former] was produced, [becomes] the Lord (*bhaṭāra*).
By the elision of the letter *ma*, one should place the *bindu* above;
this is called the "syllable of Brahmā" (*brahmākṣara*) and the "body" (*piṇḍa*) by the wise. (36)

Regarding Kaliṅanya: the Lord (Bhaṭāra) causes it to disappear; He then produces the Bindu, which is superior to the syllable Oṃ (Okāra). Such is the sequence of the arising, abiding, and dissolution of the venerable Pañcabrahma and the five-syllabled mantra.
From the letter *ma* arises the letter *a*, and from the beginning of the letter *a* arises the letter *u*.
This mantra is for the purpose of origination and is the cause of the supreme heaven. (37)
The letter *ma* is the highest; it is *tumūt a*, *tumūt u*. It is the origin of the Holy Three Syllables: *maṃ*, *aṃ*, *uṃ*. Its sequence is *ya*; it is the cause of heaven.
The letter A, the letter U, and likewise the letter M—this entire mantra of stability is considered to consist of the supreme heaven. (38)
As for the origin: *u*, *ū*, *m*; these are the abiding states of the Holy Three-Syllabled One (*tryakṣara*): *aṃ*, *uṃ*, *maṃ*. Furthermore, their sequence is heaven itself, which is its cause.
The letter *a* dissolves into the letter *u*, or indeed the letter *u* dissolves into the letter *a*;
this [syllable] *ma* is dissolved [into them], and it is proclaimed as the supreme heaven. (39)

The letter *u* dissolves upward; it dissolves into *a*; it dissolves into *m*. Thus the venerable three-syllable mantra—*uṃ*, *aṃ*, *maṃ*—is the cause of heaven (*svarga*). Furthermore, that letter *u* dissolves into the *bindu* (the dot) and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). That Lord (*bhaṭāra*) dissolves into the *nāda* (the sound). That *nāda* is other than emptiness (*śūnya*). Such is its sequence; thus is the supreme aggregate of the fourteen syllables.
This is declared to be the knowledge of differentiation, the supreme and auspicious secret;
he who knows the world and the body shall go to Śiva. (40)

May this venerable knowledge of differentiation be destroyed; let it be hidden from me, for it is the supreme secret, the secret of the world, the secret of the body. Once one has understood it, there shall be no further doubt; one attains the state of Śiva within the heart.
The state of being a celestial body is blissful, and one may easily attain nirvāṇa;
this is the secret of birth, from beginning to middle to end. (41)

O Kaliṅga, this is the divine body and this is the teaching; it is green, and it is that which is grasped by the wise man, for this knowledge is the secret of birth—its beginning, middle, and end. I shall explain it to you in its entirety, for it is supremely distinguished.

Having attained the knowledge of differentiation, the disciple— rich in faith, with senses conquered, righteous in nature, perfected in vows, devoted to the guru, and whose speech is submissive— (42).

Who is the disciple worthy to receive the venerable knowledge of differentiation (*bhedajñāna*)? A disciple who has faith in the teachings, has conquered the senses, possesses great devotion to the practice of the Dharma, is supported by his observance of vows (*vrata*), and furthermore, is devoted to his teacher. Such is his character; he is the one fit to be initiated into the venerable knowledge of differentiation. Now, the sequence [of initiation] is as follows:
The Puruṣa is traditionally described as being threefold: as possessing all [qualities], as isolated, and as pure.
Through the dissolution of the mind, he is called stainless Śiva, who is liberation. (43)

There are three characteristics of the person (*puruṣa*) in its state of conceptualization (*kalpanā*): it is *sakala* (with parts), it is *kevalaśuddha* (purely liberated), and it is *malīnatva* (tainted). This is how it is explained. *Sakala* means that he possesses the three qualities (*triguṇa*). *Kevalaśuddha* means that he has attained liberation. *Malīnatva* means that he is bound and his three qualities remain; his mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is active. *Śuddha* means the cessation of mental consciousness; because he has departed from conceptualization, this is called *yoga*. It is the state of emptiness (*śūnyākāra*) and absolute oneness (*kevalya*); he does not lose his liberation, and he is called the stainless *Śiva*.
This yogi is pure and subtle; through pure knowledge, there is liberation.
When the mind is dissolved and thoroughly purified, he is proclaimed as truly liberated. (44)

Immediately thereafter, O Sakerika, when his mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has become tranquil and still, it is free from objects, pure, and devoid of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Its form is empty, and the mind (*manas*) has vanished; this is what is called "supremely pure" (*paramaśuddha*), because it has transcended even the subtlest [states] that cannot be perceived. However, its characteristics are difficult to express. In brief: that knowledge which is pure and stainless is the condensed state of liberation. It does not arise from the mind, as it is of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyākāra*); it culminates in its dissolution. Thus, the Holy Self (*ātman*) is liberated into absolute oneness (*kaivalya*); this is what is termed the "prior limit of darkness" (*pūrvāndhakoṭi*), because there is no longer any expansion of the experience of fruits or karma. For the sake of *nirvāṇa*, he is liberated—so says the wise one.

Now, the means for attaining liberation (*mokṣa*) is as follows: there are three specific means for a person seeking liberation: the mind set on liberation (*mokṣacitta*), the established means of liberation, and its varieties, which are the triad beginning with detachment (*vairāgya*). The triad beginning with detachment consists of: external detachment (*bāhyavairāgya*), supreme detachment (*paravairāgya*), and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*). External detachment is the state of being weary [of worldly things]. One who is weary is a monk who is proficient in worldly affairs. Supreme detachment is the state of a monk who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). One who is free from passion is a monk whose mind is tranquil and blissful. Devotion to the Lord is the engagement in yoga (*ayogapravṛtti*). Engagement in yoga is a monk who is constant in his practice.

Furthermore, the triad beginning with meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of non-breath-control (*aprāṇāyāma*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and absorption (*samādhi*). Non-breath-control is the secret *kuñcī*, which is the non-returning of the exhalation. Concentration is the unification with the knowledge of the *praṇava*; unification with the knowledge of the *praṇava* is the steadying of the mind. Absorption is knowledge free from activity; knowledge free from activity is the state where there is no longer any obscuration (*kāvaraṇa*). Such is the means by which one attains here the venerable knowledge of differentiation (*bhedajñāna*).
The path of the movement of the channels is known as rebirth; those who have abandoned the channel that moves along the path are liberated and possess supreme isolation. (45)
Is it not so? The three cognitions are the waking state, and likewise the movement of the channels;
for deep sleep, there would be the three cognitions and the movement of the channels. (46)
The path of Sadāśiva is traditionally taught as the movement of the channels; the path of the supreme one is traditionally taught as the channel of the movement of the path. (47)

Thus, indeed, the venerable Lord Sadudbhrānti has spoken. And what about the venerable Lord Vyudbhrānti regarding rebirth? [The answer is: There is no mantra superior to that which is accompanied by the three syllables (*tryakṣara*) in its sequence. Furthermore, as for the method of pressing the teeth together (*dentālumakṣaṇa*), this is how the venerable Lord Sadudbhrānti grasps it, and how the venerable Lord Vyudbhrānti explains it: Furthermore, the essence of its practice is focused solely on the *pradhāna* (the primary principle). Its form is as follows: when you hear the sound of the crescent moon (*ardhacandra*), the bindu, and the *nāda*, at the moment of its arising, it is good to press the teeth together. You must restrain yourself; together with the joints and their sequence, there is the *kuñcī* (the key) within the channel (*nāḍī*) that is being pressed, as well as all the gates. Together with the breath (*vāyu*), there is the retention (*dhāraṇa*). That is *prāṇāyāma*. One must guard one's realization; do not let it be distracted. When it becomes pleasant, it is like the venerable Self (*ātman*) of living beings. It is the path of the venerable *praṇava*, ascending to the place twelve finger-breadths above. That is called the partless (*niṣkala*). It is identical with the Lord Paramaśiva; it is the very Self of Him. This is what I have declared.
Liberated from the configuration of twelve fingers, he is the supreme Śiva;
the Void alone is known as the supreme, and liberation is to be understood as arising from that. (48)

Immediately after one has emerged from the state of the twelve finger-breadths, that noble Ātman becomes united with the supreme Śiva-tattva. Regarding the term "Ātman," what is its nature? It is the void (*śūnya*) alone; it is the supreme void (*parama-śūnya*). This is how its sequence is understood by those who desire liberation. Such is the means of attainment through which the noble Mahājñāna is reached.
Liberated and having abandoned all sound, it does not go horizontally or upward, nor does it go downward; it is fruitless, empty, and absolute. (49)

The key to mastering this *sandhi* is the secret: together with *praṇāyāma*, until the end of the knowledge of the teachings (*kadhīrajñāna*), do not engage in [worldly] activity. Why is it so? Because in the body, the Lord of Life (*saṅ hyaṅ hurip*) has departed from the physical frame; it does not become impure, but rather one's consciousness becomes stainless. Yet, its fruit is not yet realized.

Now, regarding the conduct of the practitioner (*sādhaka*): even if one lacks formal worship, lacks moral discipline (*aśīla*), or lacks ritual implements (*sopacāra*), one should nevertheless contemplate the Lord (*Bhaṭāra*) Brahmā, who has four faces, three eyes, four arms, and a red complexion. One should perform *prāṇāyāma* repeatedly, closing the tip of the nose; inhale through the right nostril, and draw [the breath] down to the heart. Contemplate the Lord Brahmā, four-faced, three-eyed, four-armed, and red in color, established within the heart. *Oṃ aṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*. This is called *recaka*.

Next, one should purify the breath. Then, one should meditate upon the Great Forest (Mahāvana) and upon the nose. One should meditate upon Lord Viṣṇu, who has four arms, three eyes, and a dark complexion; one should meditate upon his installation within the nose. *Oṃ uṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. This is called *pūraka* (inhalation).

Next, one should inhale through the left nostril; hold it there for a long duration, until the breath is agitated within the abdomen. Then, meditate upon Lord Īśvara, the three-eyed, four-armed, white-complexioned Maheśvara. *Oṃ maṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*. This is called *kumbhaka*. After having done so, recite the fourteen-syllable mantra, beginning with the *praṇava*: *Oṃ saṅ baṃ taṃ aṃ iṃ naṃ maṃ śiṃ vaṃ yaṃ aṃ uṃ maṃ oṃ*. Then, exhale slowly. After that, [recite] the seed-syllable *abhasma* and *sandana*. Thus ends the brief *prāṇāyāma* worship.

Next, the fruitless [state] (viphalā). There are four kinds; their forms are as follows: desireless (niḥspṛha), extinguished (nirvāṇa), partless (niṣkala), and supportless (nirāśraya). Now, the meaning of each term: "desireless" means that there is nothing for him to accomplish. "Extinguished" means being without a body; there is nothing to be accomplished. "Partless" means that he is beyond all accumulation of elements, not subject to division, without form or color, and without hunger. He is one with the Lord and the Self (*ātman*), yet distinct from the physical body of the Lord. "Supportless" means that he transcends all conceptual knowledge, because he is the essence of the partless. Furthermore, the noble *ātman* is eternal, because it is not a material thing (*avastu*), transcending all states of being (*bhāva*), and devoid of defining characteristics (*nirlakṣaṇa*). It is truly transcendental (*paramālaukika*). Now, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) who is thus is one who, during his lifetime, does not cling to worldly things. This is because he has attained the essence of the characteristics within the fruitless state of characteristics.
First, one should perform the worldly [initiation] according to the prescribed rules for the rite of initiation;
afterwards, the supreme scholar should effect the ultimate liberation. (50)

Thus it is with the wise man (*paṇḍita*). He first performs worldly [practices]; for what is meant by "worldly" is that which is performed in this world according to the rules and procedures of initiation (*dīkṣāvidhividhāna*). Afterwards, when that is completed, he performs that supreme knowledge of absolute liberation (*paramakaivalyajñāna*). He who acts thus is the supreme wise man. Now, as for the result obtained by him: he destroys the fourfold fruit (*caturviphala*); you may see that he attains the state of liberation (*kamokṣan*). It is certain that he shall not return to birth again; because of that, there is no more substance [to rebirth], for one does not long for the bliss of liberation (*amukti-sukha*) which is without distinction [from the ultimate]. This is the means of realization (*sādhanā*) through which the fourfold fruit is attained. Do not be suspicious, for this secret is profound and difficult to understand.

The knowledge that has been explained is for the sake of liberation, which is absolute (*kaivalya*) and faultless. That *puruṣa* is absolute and without support; he is the practitioner who has been liberated from the bonds. Furthermore, when the *ṛṣis* have arrived, one should recite the sacred mantra at the navel and at the crown of the head. If it is the fourth day, [recite] at the navel and at the crown of the head. Do not let the heart become agitated or disturbed. *Kāṃ kāṃ kāṃ / a a ah*. He has been liberated by the supreme knowledge. *Oṃ śūnya*. The knowledge that has been explained is for the sake of liberation. His height is twelve finger-breadths from the *śivaketa*; *śivaketa* is the *śivaliṅga*, and the *śivaliṅga* is the hair of the head.

Furthermore, the Supreme Brahman is *Aṃ Ah*. It is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), devoid of duality, and is purely formless, characterized by the sound *Aṃ*. It pervades the body, residing within the nine gates; the body is empty in form when [the breath] has ceased. This is what I call *Sūryasmṛti* (the remembrance of the Sun). When *Ah* vibrates through the wind (*vāyu*) of the body, the body takes on the form of the Moon (*candrarūpa*). When the wind in the body ceases, the body remains as a gentle, cool radiance. This is what I call *Śāntacandra* (the Tranquil Moon), the remembrance which is thus. Furthermore, when both *Sūryasmṛti* and *Candrasmṛti* become the knowledge of *Praṇava*, that person merges with the Lord Supreme Brahman and the Lord Praṇavajñāna. He is eternally established in the form of light, forever without obstruction, like the brilliance of a *maṇikamanta* jewel, illuminating many regions and shining constantly without setting. His fragrance is not to be sought after, for he is the pure *Śivasmṛti*. If one should behold him, it is this very *Aṃ Ah*. He is called "immediately transcendent" (*sadyodbhrānti*). He is the Supreme Brahman, the father of Lord Śiva. Furthermore, regarding this knowledge: knowing without conceptualization, formless and radiant—this is what is called the Lord Praṇavajñāna. He is Lord Bhaumaśiva; he possesses Sājñavaśīśvarī. Therefore, the *Praṇavajñāna* is known as the *Tridevī* (the Triple Goddess); she is the mother of Lord Śiva.
O son, it is of that very same form. The form of Lord Śiva is nothing other than Maṅkana. When is the form of Lord Jyoti? It is Maṅkana, the Liṅga, the venerable Lord Saṃsipta.
The letter *u* dissolves into the letter *o*, and the letter *a* dissolves [into *u*];
the letter *m* is absorbed into the *bindu*, and the *bindu* dissolves into the *nāda*. (51)
And the *nāda* dissolves into the void; thus the void itself arises.
Even beyond the void, there is that which is characterized by absolute emptiness. (52)
The Sakala, the Sakalatattva, the Sūkṣma, the Sakalaniṣkala, the Para, the Niṣkala, the Śūnya, the Ūrdhvātyūrdhva, and the Atyśūnyaka. (53)
Thus concludes the *Saṅ hyaṅ Praṇavajñāna*, concerning liberation from desire.
The venerable Lord of Umā,
Praṇavaśrīdevī, Oṃ Śrīdevī Sarasvatī.

The head is supreme Śiva, the emptiness of the void; the place of the twelve fingers is the head. *Haṃsa* is the cause, *praṇava* is the effect; *sadāśiva* is the function of *haṃsa*. *Īśvara*, *brahmā*, and *viṣṇu* are the manifestations of the knowledge of *praṇava* regarding liberation.
Oṃ, Śiva, the ground of absolute emptiness and supreme void; Oṃ, the partless void within the void at the root of the throat; Oṃ, the void that is both with and without parts in the chest.
The entire [universe] is the abode of the navel, A-U.

4. Now follows the entry of the venerable Śiva: he who causes the birth of his [manifestations]. The venerable Śiva resides in the eyes; his appearance is like molten gold. He is the self (ātman) of sight. He is the venerable Pramāṇa; he resides at the tip of the nose, above the root of the tongue; his appearance is pale. He is the self of hearing. The venerable Jñāna resides in the hollow of the ears; his appearance is white and free from impurity. He is the divine self (devātman) of thought. Furthermore, when there is the sensation of touch, the venerable Śiva, the venerable Pramāṇa, and the venerable Jñāna are unified. Such is the path of the venerable Śiva.

Furthermore, regarding the gatekeeper: he is unborn and does not experience suffering; the venerable Śivātman together with his body is unborn here, yet he is the one who carries [the soul] across. Now, as for what is called "carrying across": at the upper level it is seven, and at the lower level it is two; this is the smallest gate. If it is a gate at the Śivadvāra, it is in the middle. Moreover, that supreme path is the way of the venerable Śivātman. In the height of sound, it is easy to perceive within the heart; if one practices it during the *kalpasan* (meditative session), the body becomes unborn and divine, and the disciples also attain bliss. These three aspects are unified; thus one attains the height of sound, which is easy to perceive. Thus ends the *kalpasan* of Saṅ Bhujaṅgaśiva. Do not let the secret be destroyed; otherwise, its fruit will not be realized.

6. Thus is the Holy Supreme Instruction: At the time when there is no world (*bhuvana*), there is no unevenness or curvature; there is no emptiness-nirvāṇa; there is no knowledge (*jñāna*); there is no distinction (*viśeṣa*); there is none of all these. That which is the support of the *samana* breath is the locus of supreme bliss (*paramasukha*). It is not bliss by means of emptiness, nor is it the absence of emptiness; it is not bliss by means of nirvāṇa, nor is it the absence of nirvāṇa; it is not bliss by means of knowledge, nor is it the absence of knowledge; it is not bliss by means of distinction, nor is it the absence of distinction. It is solely the state of supreme bliss itself, without interior, without middle, without form, without color, and without stone (solidity). It is subtle and cannot be described; it is not bliss by means of sound, nor is it the absence of sound; it is not bliss by means of touch, nor is it the absence of touch. It is solely inconceivable bliss as its body. From that inconceivable bliss arises the Holy One of Knowledge and Distinction (*jñānaviśeṣa*). He is not found in the inferior, for he is the essence of knowledge; he is not a distinction, for he is the essence of distinction. He is not found in emptiness, for he is the essence of emptiness; he is not found in nirvāṇa, for he is the essence of nirvāṇa; he is not found in the essence of the world, for he is the essence of the world; he is not found in the most subtle, for he is the essence of the subtle. Such is the Holy One of Knowledge and Distinction, who is named the Holy Cause of the World (*jagatkāraṇa*).

7. O Maṅke, the Lord who is the cause of the world (*jagatkāraṇa*) does not yet appear when the fire of dissolution (*avakirāgana*) has subsided, as long as he is not yet released from his body. He is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*). The relationship between cause and effect is reciprocal: one is *sakala* while the other is *niṣkala*. Such is the manner of it: He makes emptiness (*śūnya*) His abode for the manifestation of His creative power (*klir*). He is not aware of that act of creation. Once the Lord who is the cause of the world has finished [His work], the effect of His creation arises, taking its place within emptiness. Such is the manner of it: Nirvāṇa arises; from Nirvāṇa arises the pure *oṃkāra*; from the pure *oṃkāra* emerges the sound (*svara*), from which arises the *bindu-prāṇa*, the color of pure crystal. Within it is the *nādaprāṇa*, the purity of primordial wisdom (*jñānaśuddha*). Its form is like the shimmering clusters of the sun and moon; its radiance is such. Thus is the *bindu-prāṇa*. The *nādaprāṇa* arises from the pure *oṃkāra*.

8. O Noble One, Oṃkāraśuddha Praṇavajñāna, I shall explain the origin of the mantras of the Vedas as the body of the Supreme Being. The Supreme Being is that which is to be honored, the *bindu-prāṇa*. Its manifestation is as follows: from the *bindu-prāṇa* arises the *karas* (the hands); from the *nāda-prāṇa* arises the *tanah* (the feet). From these arise the syllables (*akṣara*). Their manifestations are as follows: from *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa* arises the *matmahan* (the head); from *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa* arise *ca, cha, ja, jha, ña*, which is the *matmahan* of the *dagiṅ* (the chest), joined together like the hilt of a sword; from *ca, cha, ja, jha, ña* arise *ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa*, which is the *matmahan* of the *kulit* (the skin); from *ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa* arise *ta, tha, da, dha, na*, which is the *matmahan* of the *hodod* (the flesh); from *ta, tha, da, dha, na* arise *pa, pha, ba, bha, ma*, which is the *matmahan* of the *asthi* (the bones); from *pa, pha, ba, bha, ma* arise *ya, ra, la, va*, which is the *matmahan* of the *sumsum* (the marrow); from *ya, ra, la, va* arise *śa, ṣa, sa, ha*, which is the *matmahan* of the *huntĕk* (the extremities). Such is the origin of the single syllable (*ekākṣara*), whose form is like the *śivaliṅga*.

9. Now, regarding the single-syllable [mantras] that become three-syllable [mantras], their manifestations (*lvirnya*) are as follows: *a* and *ā* manifest as the head; *i* and *ī* manifest as the tongue; *u* and *ū* manifest as the chin; *ṛ* and *ḥ* manifest as the eyes; *ḷ* and *ḹ* manifest as the nostrils; *e* and *ai* manifest as the palate; *o* and *au* manifest as the throat and neck. Beyond this is the recitation of the syllables below: *ka* manifests as the pubic region (*caṇṭik*); *kha* manifests as the *mūlādhāra*; *ga* manifests as the anus; *gha* manifests as the rectum (*pāyu*); *ṅa* manifests as the genitals (*upastha*, *kontol*). *ca* manifests as the lips and the jaw; *cha* manifests as the teeth and the gums; *ja* manifests as the palms and the feet; *jha* manifests as the nails; *ña* manifests as the fingernails and the hair of the hands and feet, and likewise within the middle [of the body]. *ṭa* manifests as the navel; *ṭha* manifests as the lower back; *ḍa* manifests as the depth of the secret place (*guhya*); *ḍha* manifests as the liver; *ṇa* manifests as the spleen. *ta* manifests as the shoulders; *tha* manifests as the chest; *da* manifests as the stomach; *dha* manifests as the kidneys; *na* manifests as the heart. *pa* manifests as the breasts; *pha* manifests as the ribs; *ba* manifests as the buttocks; *bha* manifests as the arms, hands, and nails; *ma* manifests as the elbows. *ya* manifests as the throat; *ra* manifests as the palate; *la* manifests as the tongue; *va* manifests as the pubic region (*caṇṭik*). *śa* manifests as the upper lip and the cheeks; *ṣa* manifests as the tip of the tongue; *sa* manifests as the lower lip and the chin; *ha* manifests as the heart, the channels (*nāḍī*), and the fruit of the vital breaths (*suratādhikaphala*), including the hair of the head and body. Such are the manifestations of these [syllables]. This is the function of the Noble One (*saṅ hyaṅ*), the knowledge of the pure *praṇava* *oṃkāra*.

Ten *ri* (finger-widths) above the crown of the head is the Noble One, the Cause of the World (*jagatkāraṇa*). Beyond that, He manifests as the *karyyātmā* (the active self) from His own body, establishing Himself in various places. Such are their forms: Brahmā resides in the *mūlādhāra*; His color is yellow (*pīta-varṇa*), and He guards the marrow. Viṣṇu resides in the navel; His color is black (*kṛṣṇa-varṇa*), and He guards the blood. Rudra resides in the heart; His color is red (*rakta-varṇa*), and He guards the skin. Īśvara resides in the throat; His color is white (*śveta-varṇa*), and He guards the saliva. Sadāśiva resides at the tip of the tongue; His color is like pure crystal (*śuddhasphaṭika-varṇa*), and He guards the hair of the head. Such is the form of the *ātman* established in these various places.

From the self (ātman), the fifteen sense-faculties (indriya) arise; from the ten sense-faculties, those five homas and the five tīrthas arise. That which is the *mūlādhāra* is the Great Bindu, the color of pure crystal. That bindu ascends into the body of the world (*bhuvanaśarīra*). It proceeds by way of the navel (*nābhi*). That bindu is Śiva; from Śiva, human beings arise. Such is the manner in which humans are produced. This is the *bhuvanaśarīra*. This is the teaching of the great one who possesses the *liṅga*.

12. Herein lies the Lotus Wheel (*kamalacakra*). The heart is my *pusuhpusuh* (the central channel); Nīlakaṇṭha is my throat. Nīlakaṇṭha is the tip; the *gavikā* (the uvula) is its dark-blue color at the base of the tip. The *lambikā* (the tongue) is the bulb of the tip. The Lord of the Tenth Day (*daśamīsara*) is the core of the throat. *Dhryāgaulaṣṭhā* is the root of the palate. The thousand-petaled lotus is the crown of the head. The venerable *Nādaprakāśa* is the hair. The venerable *Niṣkala* is the droplet (*bindu*) atop the hair. Thus, the Great Tantra of the State is the locus of the secret. Through wisdom, by means of mental concentration, through the differentiation of the heart-mind, and through union with the secret within the secret. It is the sovereign distinction within the heart. It is the resting place of the venerable Suparṇṇi. He who is the supreme essence is the Goddess Sarasvatī. She is the remover of the impurities of the body, like water within the heart. She is the one who purifies the impurities of birth.

13. Herein is the specific mantra consisting of five syllables (*pañcākṣara*). Its form is: *namaḥ śivāya*. *Namaḥ* is praise to the Lord together with Śiva. *Śi* is the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*); *vā* is the principle of Sadāśiva (*sadāśivatattva*); *ya* is the principle of Paramaśiva (*paramaśivatattva*). The reason this five-syllable mantra is practiced by the Brahmin Bhujaṅga, the Śaiva, and the Sogata (Buddhist), who are proficient in the principles, observances, scriptures, and the three-syllable mantra *aṃ uṃ maṃ*, is as follows: *aṃ* is Śivayoga, the Śiva-mantra, and the Śiva-principle; *uṃ* is Sadāśivayoga, the worship of Sadāśiva, and the Sadāśiva-principle; *maṃ* is Paramaśivayoga, the recitation (*japa*) of Paramaśiva, and the Paramaśiva-principle. Furthermore, there is another three-syllable mantra: *aṃ ah hrīḥ*. *Aṃ* is Śiva; *ah* is Sadāśiva; *hrīḥ* is Paramaśiva. This is the extensive secret; the scriptures have been concealed. Such is the mantra.

And there are the five-syllable and three-syllable mantras; the mantra known as *bhasma* (ashes), *mvaḥ* (water), which when performed makes one pure (*pavitra*), and furthermore [removes] all diseases, all impurities, all calamities, all evils, and all weapons. That which is established in all *liṅgas* is that which does not perish even when it enters the head. And its seed-syllable (*vījakṣara*) is the root-syllable (*mūlākṣara*) of the scripture: *ha*. This syllable *ha* is what is taught in the scripture as both the conscious (*cetana*) and the unconscious (*acetana*). It is the essence of oneness (*ekatva*), the essence of the union of speech and mind, and the essence of the *oṃkāra* together with its vowels and consonants. This *ha* is the supreme Śiva, who is the very embodiment of the scripture.

15. Day after day, the noble one experiences suffering within the body; this must be examined. If he is separated from the body, the body indeed becomes happy. When that happiness has ceased, then his head and his trunk—within the state of perfect discernment—he reflects: "Who am I? Who is mine? He perceives that his body is merely a vessel for the sake of Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Paramaśiva. "The Self of Śiva is on my right side; the Self of Sadāśiva is on my left side; the Self of Paramaśiva is in all [the limbs]."

For seventeen days, one should practice yogic sleep (yoganidrā) while focusing on the tip of the nose. This is the means for attaining subtle knowledge (*sūkṣmajñāna*), which is indeed nothing other than meditation (*dhyāna*). By this, the enemy that is death disappears; likewise, the mind’s perversity (*viparīta*) vanishes. All mental afflictions (*manaravaṅ*) are destroyed, and one attains a particular excellence of knowledge (*jñānaviśeṣa*). One may even contemplate one's own body from within its interior, because it serves as the locus for liberation (*mokṣa*).

Furthermore, you must be able to merge into the Mahāpraṇava. There is no distinction between the body and the three worlds. To explain this: that which is the Holy Mahāpraṇava is the essence of the worlds (*bhuvanātmaka*), yet it exists apart from the worlds. It is *Paramārdhānareśvarī*; it is the source from which the Holy Ātman seeks liberation. That is the Holy Niṣkala, whose name is Bindu. The utterance of mantras is devoid of it; its seed-syllable is the letter *ya*, belonging to the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*). It has gone to that which seeks the supportless (*nirāśraya*). It is easy for one to know it; all sins reside within it. It does not eat; it does not possess a "I" (*ahaṃ*); it does not desire; it does not differentiate between what is evil and what is good. It knows the internal difference between speech and forgetfulness. You may sleep, O one who knows yogic sleep (*yoganidrā*), for speech is merely a manifestation of the mind.

19. Herein lies the summary: it concerns both the conscious (*cetana*) and the unconscious (*acetana*). Its form is as follows: the state of good and evil within the unconscious; furthermore, the state of all the sense faculties when they have lost their respective objects; and subsequently, the function of the *tattva* (principle) of *tutur* (instruction), which is the void (*śūnya*) that is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), the state of the conscious (*cetana*) which is luminous (*prakāśa*). It is said: "It is attained through the cessation of ignorance by means of specific knowledge (*jñānaviśeṣa*); for that cessation of ignorance is what is attained upon reaching the state of liberation. He indeed departs to the state of Śiva, which is his name. It is said: thus ends the *Praṇavaṭīkā*, the inner instruction.
The syllable *jaḥ* should be known as earth; the syllable *taḥ* is established as water.

*Na-dya-ta-ya / Jaḥ / Taḥ / Kiṃ / Uṃ / Phaṭ*. This is the *pañcakāṇḍa* of the Holy Lord; by reciting it while meditating on Śiva, one destroys the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). *Aṃ Ah*, recite this sixteen times while meditating on Śiva; its fruit is stainless purity. That which is meditation on Supreme Śiva has liberation as its fruit. That which is most excellent in the midst of battle is meditation on Rudra. That which is most excellent for the prosperity of the kingdom is meditation on Mahādeva. That which is most excellent for accomplishing all tasks is meditation on Śaṅkara. That which is most excellent for destroying rebirth is, furthermore, meditation on Īśvara. *Aṃ* is the seed-syllable of the Self (*ātman*); *Ah* is the seed-syllable of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*); their great union is this. Do not let it be lost. This is the Great Recitation (*mahājapa*) of the Holy Lord; it is the supreme secret. 0 // 0 // 0 //

Next, the *kadgarāvaṇa* [mantra]: *oṃ ha ka śa ma la va ra yaṃ uṃ*. This is called the *ardhanārīśvara* [mantra]. Regarding the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the sequence of circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇākrama*), and the *andĕlakna* [placement] upon the *padmahṛdaya*, it is as follows: in the intermediate directions (*vidikvidik*). What is the fruit of all that has been produced? It is the removal of all obstacles (*sarvavighna*). This is the ritual application (*anuṣṭhāna*) of the *nyāsa* for the venerable *mṛtyuñjaya*: *oṃ* at the gate of Śiva (*śivadvāra*); *aṃ* at the face (*vaktra*); *kaṃ* at the throat (*kaṇṭha*); *ah* at the inner heart (*antarhṛdaya*); *aṃ* at the navel (*nābhi*); *tkeṅ* on both feet. This is connected with the venerable ten-syllable mantra (*daśākṣaramantra*): *oṃ auṃ ha ka śa ma loa va ra ya m uṃ / namo namah svāhā*. This is the *sīkadhī* and the *padāntanyāsa*. *Smah*. Next is the mantra: *oṃ maṃ sah vauṣaṭ / mṛtyuñjayāya namah svāhā vaṣaṭ*.

Herein is the description of Gaṇapati: his body is white; he has a trunk; he wears a garland of *gaṇa* seeds; his left hand holds a discus (*cakra*), and his right hand holds a mace (*gadā*). His forehead is adorned with a white and yellow tilaka; he wears a pure lower garment (*asoroh*) and a white upper cloth (*pithik*) reaching to his knees. His vehicle is a bull (*saṅku tmagā*). His mantra is *skar sudhāmala saha prasasantun*. Its numerical value is 1100. Recite it one thousand times. After the recitation is finished, place these seed-syllables (*rajahan*) upon the bull. On the day of worship, scatter them upon the sacrificial ground (*kamraṇan*). Ma. (End.)
Oṃ! Gaṇapati, the son of Śiva, who has partaken of the sacrificial offering;
he who is honored throughout the world, possessing a body that is pure and complete; the destroyer of all poisons; the one whose gaze is like Time itself, the Lord of the *dṛṅgas*. (57)
To the one who subdues other diseases, who is the source of sustenance for the three worlds,
who grants the accomplishment of the *gaṅgā* and *gomaya* mantras, who is the teacher of the hosts of gods, and whose son is [Śiva]—
may his grace that bestows gain prevail for the sake of power, heroism, light, and glory. (58–59)
